# Design Objectives — The 8+1 Whole-Building Goals (WBDG) Reference guidance on the design objectives a high-performance building must balance. Source: WBDG Design Objectives. Best-practice guidance (how to think about a design), not a regulation or binding standard — the project brief and the client's requirements govern priorities. International practice, applies to KSA. These objectives are interdependent: a good design integrates them rather than optimising one in isolation. Grounds how the platform reasons about design trade-offs and brief/BOD analysis. ## The design objectives## The design objectives | Objective | What it means | |---|---| | Accessible | Usable by people of all abilities; accessible routes, entrances, and facilities (universal design). | | Aesthetics | The form, materials, and image of the building and its fit with context. | | Cost-Effective | Best value over the whole life cycle — life-cycle cost, not lowest first cost; value engineering. | | Functional / Operational | Meets the functional programme; systems integration, flexibility, durability, operability. | | Historic Preservation | Respects historic/existing fabric; adaptive reuse where relevant. | | Productive | Occupant comfort, health, and productivity — thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, indoor air quality, ergonomics. | | Resilient | Resists and recovers from hazards and disruptions — robustness, redundancy, adaptability. | | Secure / Safe | Physical security, life safety, fire protection, and natural-hazard mitigation. | | Sustainable | Environmental performance — energy, water, materials, site, and indoor environmental quality (the home of LEED-type goals). |Source: WBDG Design Objectives. ## How they work together - The objectives are **interdependent** — decisions for one affect others (e.g. a sustainability move can improve productivity but change cost). A high-performance design evaluates and balances them, it does not maximise one alone. - **Cost-Effective** is judged on **whole-life cost** (life-cycle cost analysis), not first cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count.ost — durability, energy, and maintenance count. - **Sustainable** is where rating systems (e.g. LEED) live; WBDG frames the goal, the specific rating credits are a separate standard. ## How to use - Use this to explain what each objective covers and that they must be balanced. - The project brief / Owner's Project Requirements set the priority weighting for a specific project — this is the general framework. - When analysing a brief or basis of design, check which objectives are addressed and flag gaps (e.g. resilience or accessibility not mentioned) rather than inventing requirements.

# Design Review and Acceptance Procedure ## Scope The design review and acceptance procedure governs the review and acceptance of design documents within the construction programme. It applies to all design submissions from consultants, architects, and engineers. ## Valid Design Review Statuses Only these statuses are permitted on design documents under the design review procedure:ign documents under the design review procedure: - `FOR_COMMENT` — issued for review and feedback - `ACCEPTANCE` — accepted for use without further comment - `BUY_OFF` — closed-out / agreed; no further iteration required - `PENDING_DEBRIEF` — awaiting formal debrief meeting - `SUPERSEDED` — replaced by a newer revision Plain-language equivalents permitted on the title block: `accepted`, `for comment`, `buy-off`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documentsoff`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documents These statuses are contractually prohibited on design documents and must never appear on design submissions: - `APPROVED` - `APPROVAL` - `SIGN_OFF` ### Why APPROVED Is Forbidden The word `APPROVED` carries contractual liability. It implies that the reviewer has accepted the design and assumes responsibility for its content. The design review procedure explicitly prohibits this word on design documents to preserve the contractor's liability for design correctness. Use `accepted`, `for comment`, or `buy-off` instead. ### What This Means In Practice - A QA officer who stamps a structural drawing `APPROVED` is non-compliant with the design review procedure. The drawing must be re-stamped with one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cath one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cannot use `APPROVED` regardless of seniority — the prohibition applies to all signatories. - The same rule applies to `APPROVAL` and `SIGN_OFF`. ## Review Distribution Period ### Minimum Distribution Period Design review packages must be distributed to relevant stakeholders at least **7 calendar days** before the scheduled Design Review Workshop. This is a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant.s a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant. The 7-day figure is **calendar days**, not business days. Weekends and public holidays count toward the period. ### Maximum Distribution Period The design review procedure recommends a maximum distribution period of 14 calendar days. Distributing too far in advance encourages stakeholders to defer review and can dilute attention. ### Common Misconceptioncan dilute attention. ### Common Misconception The minimum review period is **not 30 days**. Some teams cite 30 days from other procedures or contract clauses; the design review procedure is explicit on 7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Example If the Design Review Workshop is scheduled for the 15th of the month, the review pack must be issued no later than the 8th of that month. Distributing on the 8th gives exactly 7 calendar days before the 15th.h gives exactly 7 calendar days before the 15th. If the pack is distributed only 3 calendar days before the workshop, the workshop must be postponed by at least 4 additional calendar days to comply. ## Related Procedures - Design directive procedure — Design Directives and Employer Approval - Change management procedure — Variation Orders vs Request for Modification (RFM) - Non-conformance procedure — Non-Conformance Reports (NCR)

# Excavations & Trenching — Site Safety Criteria (OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P) REAL, sourced excavation and trenching thresholds for construction sites. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652 (Subpart P) plus Appendix B, US federal regulation, public domain. US-reference standard: in Saudi Arabia site HSE is governed by Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project HSE plan, not OSHA, but Saudi practice broadly aligns. Note that Gulf ground conditions (sabkha, collapsible and high-water-table soils) often demand stricter shoring than the generic soil types below — always defer to the project geotechnical report. Values are metric-led (SI) with the original US-customary figure in parentheses. ## Access, egress and edge protection## Access, egress and edge protection | Requirement | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Depth at which egress (ladder/ramp/stairway) is required | 1.22 m | 4 ft | | Maximum lateral travel to egress in a trench | 7.62 m | 25 ft | | Minimum distance to keep spoil/materials from the edge | 0.61 m | 2 ft |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(c)(2), (j)(2). ## When a protective system is required## When a protective system is required | Requirement | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Depth requiring a protective system (unless in stable rock) | 1.52 m | 5 ft | | Depth above which the system must be designed by a registered engineer | 6.09 m | 20 ft |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652(a), (b); Appendix B to Subpart P. Below 1.52 m a competent person may exempt an excavation only if examination shows no cave-in potential. ## Maximum allowable slopes by soil type (simple slope)## Maximum allowable slopes by soil type (simple slope) | Soil type | Max slope (H:V) | Angle from horizontal | |---|---|---| | Stable rock | Vertical | 90° | | Type A | 3/4 : 1 | 53° | | Type B | 1 : 1 | 45° | | Type C | 1½ : 1 | 34° |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1. Slopes are for excavations up to 6.09 m (20 ft) deep; deeper cuts must be engineer-designed. Soil type is set by a competent person; where types are uncertain, use the more conservative (Type C). ## Inspection and water - A competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas, and protective systems before each shift, as needed through the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event.ery rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event. - Work is not permitted in an excavation with accumulated water unless adequate precautions (support/shielding, water removal and monitoring, safety harness and lifeline) are taken. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(h), (k). ## KSA applicability OSHA 1926 is a US-reference standard, not the governing authority in Saudi Arabia (site HSE is under Saudi labour law / MHRSD and the project HSE plan).udi labour law / MHRSD and the project HSE plan). THE OPERATIONAL VOLTAGE FOR EACH LUMINAIRE IS 230V AND THE LIGHTING LUMINARIES SHALL BE EQUALLY DISTRIBUTED ON THREE PHASES. 4. THE VOLTAGE FOR STREET LIGHTING CIRCUITS SHALL BE 400/230 VOLTS. 5. ALL STREET LIGHTING CABLES SHALL BE MULTI CORE, COPPER, XLPE / PVC / SWA. DIRECTLY BURIED. 6. SYSTEM PARAMETERS FOR 400V SYSTEM SHALL BE AS FOLLOWS, A. AMBIENT TEMPERATURE- 50°C B. NOMINAL VOLTAGE - 400V/230V C. HIGHEST VOLTAGE – 420/241.5V D. SYSTEM FREQUENCY- 60HZ E. SYSTEM POWER FREQUENCY WITHSTAND VOLTAGE- 4kV 7. 20% SPARE QUANTITY OF FEEDERS SHALL BE CONSIDERED IN EACH STREET LIGHTING FEEDER PANEL. 8. IN THE INCOMER SIDE OF EACH STREET LIGHTING FEEDER PANEL RCCB FOR LEAKAGE CURRENT PROTECTION WITH 100mA SETTING SHALL BE PROVIDED. 9. FOR ROAD CROSSING ALL CABLES SHALL BE ROUTED THROUGH uPVC DUCT BANK. ROAD CROSSING DUCT BANKS SHALL BE CONCRETE ENCASED. 10. THE PERMISSIBLE VOLTAGE DROP FROM SOURCE (TRANSFORMER) TO THE LAST LUMINAIRE IN THE STREET LIGHTING CIRCUIT SHALL NOT EXCEED 5% IF IT IS FED THROUGH FEEDER PILLAR. 11. THE COLOR TEMPERATURE FOR STREET LIGHTING SYSTEM SHOULD BE USED ACCORDING TO LOCAL MUNICIPALITY REQUIREMENTS: - 3000 KELVIN FOR MAIN ROADS. HOWEVER THE COLOR TEMPERATURE FOR STREET LIGHTING LUMINARIES SHALL BE APPROVED FROM THE RELATED MUNICIPALITY / SUPERVISOR ENGINEER BEFORE THE LUMINARIES ARE SUPPLIED. THE COLOR TEMPERATURE SELECTED FOR THE DETAIL PHASE ARE PRELIMINARIES AND WILL BE UPDATED UPON RELATIVE AUTHORITY COMMENTS AND CLIENT/CLIENT REPRESENTATIVE COMMENTS. 12. THE STREET LIGHTING LAYOUTS ARE PROVISIONAL, FINAL LAYOUTS/ CONSTRUCTION DRAWINGS WILL BE PREPARED BY THE CONTRACTOR AFTER COORDINATING WITH OTHER DISCIPLINES AND AS PER ACTUAL SITE CONDITION AND WILL GET APPROVAL FROM CLIENT PRIOR TO THE EXECUTION OF WORK. 13. ALL LIGHTING POLE PROPOSED IN THE LAYOUT ARE TENTATIVE ONLY,THE CONTRACTOR SHALL SUBMIT A PROPOSAL TO THE OWNER ALONG WITH ORIGINAL CATALOGUES AND SHALL PROCURE THE POLE /LUMINARIES ONLY AFTER GETTING THE APPROVAL FROM THE OWNER. 14. SINCE LED EFFICIENCY i.e LUMIN PER WATT IS IMPROVING WITH THE PASSAGE OF TIME. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE LED LUMINARIES WITH STATE OF THE ART TECHNOLOGY AVAILABLE AT THE TIME OF INSTALLATION KEEPING THE SAME ACHIEVED ILLUMINES LEVEL. 15. DUCT BANK ROUTING/ NO. OF uPVC PIPES SHOWN HERE ARE TENTATIVE, SHALL BE FINALIZED BY CONTRACTOR DURING CONSTRUCTION DRAWING STAGE AND AS PER ACTUAL REQUIREMENT AT SITE. 16. THE uPVC CONDUIT SHALL BE SEALED WITH NON FLAMMABLE SEALING COMPOUND. 17. DIMMING CONTROL IS SUBJECT TO CLIENT AND RELATIVE AUTHORITY APPROVAL. 18.STREET LIGHTING CONTROL SCHEME TO BE COORDINATED WITH THE SMART CITIES TEAM. A

Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. # Stairways & Ladders — Site Safety Criteria (OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart X) REAL, sourced stairway and ladder thresholds for construction sites. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1052 (stairways) and 1926.1053 (ladders), Subpart X, US federal regulation, public domain. US-reference standard: in Saudi Arabia site HSE is governed by Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project HSE plan, not OSHA, but Saudi practice broadly aligns. Values are metric-led (SI) with the original US-customary figure in parentheses. ## Ladders## Ladders | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Extension above the upper landing surface | 0.9 m | 3 ft | | Set-up pitch (base distance ≈ ¼ of working length) | 4 : 1 (75° approx) | 4 : 1 | | Rung / step spacing | 25–36 cm | 10–14 in | | Minimum clear width between side rails (portable) | 29 cm | 11½ in | | Minimum perpendicular clearance behind rungs | 18 cm | 7 in | | Load capacity (safety factor) | 4× intended load | 4× intended load |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1053(a)–(b). ## Stairways## Stairways | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Stairrails/handrails required at | 4+ risers or rise > 76 cm | 4+ risers or > 30 in | | Handrail height above tread | 76–94 cm | 30–37 in | | Stairrail top-edge height (systems after 15 Mar 1991) | ≥ 91.5 cm | ≥ 36 in | | Maximum vertical rise between landings | 3.7 m | 12 ft | | Riser height / tread depth uniformity tolerance | ≤ 0.6 cm | ≤ ¼ in | | Permitted stairway angle from horizontal | 30°–50° | 30°–50° |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1052(a)–(c). ## KSA applicability OSHA 1926 is a US-reference standard, not the governing authority in Saudi Arabia (site HSE is under Saudi labour law / MHRSD and the project HSE plan). Saudi practice broadly aligns on ladder extension above landing, the 4:1 set-up pitch, and stairrail heights. Where a value is enforced on site, confirm it against the project HSE plan. ## How to use - Quote the SI value for site use; cite the US original and the regulation number so the basis is traceable. - The project HSE plan and the equipment manufacturer's data take precedence over these reference figures. - State that this is a US-reference figure, not the governing authority for a Saudi project.

# Excavations & Trenching — Site Safety Criteria (OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P) REAL, sourced excavation and trenching thresholds for construction sites. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652 (Subpart P) plus Appendix B, US federal regulation, public domain. US-reference standard: in Saudi Arabia site HSE is governed by Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project HSE plan, not OSHA, but Saudi practice broadly aligns. Note that Gulf ground conditions (sabkha, collapsible and high-water-table soils) often demand stricter shoring than the generic soil types below — always defer to the project geotechnical report. Values are metric-led (SI) with the original US-customary figure in parentheses. ## Access, egress and edge protection## Access, egress and edge protection | Requirement | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Depth at which egress (ladder/ramp/stairway) is required | 1.22 m | 4 ft | | Maximum lateral travel to egress in a trench | 7.62 m | 25 ft | | Minimum distance to keep spoil/materials from the edge | 0.61 m | 2 ft |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(c)(2), (j)(2). ## When a protective system is required## When a protective system is required | Requirement | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Depth requiring a protective system (unless in stable rock) | 1.52 m | 5 ft | | Depth above which the system must be designed by a registered engineer | 6.09 m | 20 ft |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652(a), (b); Appendix B to Subpart P. Below 1.52 m a competent person may exempt an excavation only if examination shows no cave-in potential. ## Maximum allowable slopes by soil type (simple slope)## Maximum allowable slopes by soil type (simple slope) | Soil type | Max slope (H:V) | Angle from horizontal | |---|---|---| | Stable rock | Vertical | 90° | | Type A | 3/4 : 1 | 53° | | Type B | 1 : 1 | 45° | | Type C | 1½ : 1 | 34° |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1. Slopes are for excavations up to 6.09 m (20 ft) deep; deeper cuts must be engineer-designed. Soil type is set by a competent person; where types are uncertain, use the more conservative (Type C). ## Inspection and water - A competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas, and protective systems before each shift, as needed through the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event.y rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event. - Work is not permitted in an excavation with accumulated water unless adequate precautions (support/shielding, water removal and monitoring, safety harness and lifeline) are taken. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(h), (k). ## KSA applicability OSHA 1926 is a US-reference standard, not the governing authority in Saudi Arabia (site HSE is under Saudi labour law / MHRSD and the project HSE plan).di labour law / MHRSD and the project HSE plan). ALJAZZAR g) ip ot I MOHAMMED OMAR JAZZAR CONSULTING ENGINEERS CO Auwsigl GILaiuS Ne ae dane AS yc 1. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. # EVM Thresholds and Traffic Light System ## CPI and SPI — Definitions **CPI (Cost Performance Index)** = EV ÷ AC - CPI > 1.0 means cost efficient — earned value exceeds actual cost. - CPI = 1.0 means on budget. - CPI < 1.0 means over budget — earned value is less than actual cost. **SPI (Schedule Performance Index)** = EV ÷ PV (also expressed as BCWP ÷ BCWS) - SPI > 1.0 means ahead of schedule. - SPI = 1.0 means on schedule. - SPI < 1.0 means behind schedule.on schedule. - SPI < 1.0 means behind schedule. Interpretation note: an SPI of 0.8 means the project has earned only 80 cents of value for every dollar planned. An SPI below 1.0 always means the project is behind schedule. ## CPI Traffic Light System The CPI Traffic Light is the standard executive-dashboard rule: - **GREEN — CPI > 1.00** — Under Budget, Cost Efficient. Keep doing what works. - **AMBER — 0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** — Slightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action.lightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action. - **RED — CPI < 0.90** — Over Budget, Cost Inefficient. Take corrective action now. The RED threshold is **CPI < 0.90**. Anything below 0.90 is RED. The AMBER band is **0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** (inclusive on both ends). A CPI of exactly 0.90 is AMBER. A CPI of exactly 1.00 is AMBER. The GREEN band is **CPI > 1.00** (strictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examplestrictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examples - CPI of 0.85 → RED (below the 0.90 threshold). - CPI of 0.91 → AMBER (above 0.90, within the 0.90-1.00 band). - CPI of 0.93 → AMBER. - CPI of 0.95 → AMBER. - CPI of 1.05 → GREEN (above 1.00). - CPI of 0.72 → RED. Action required: forensic cost-variance analysis and a recovery plan. The project is materially overspending against earned value. ## SPI Traffic Light Systemainst earned value. ## SPI Traffic Light System - **GREEN — SPI > 1.00** — Ahead of Schedule. Maintain momentum. - **AMBER — 0.90 ≤ SPI ≤ 1.00** — Slightly Behind. Review plan and recover. - **RED — SPI < 0.90** — Behind Schedule, At Risk. Take corrective action now. ## Combined CPI / SPI Interpretation Both indices together describe project health: - CPI > 1.0 AND SPI > 1.0 → Ahead and under budget. Great performance. - CPI < 1.0 AND SPI > 1.0 → Ahead but over budget. Monitor costs.SPI > 1.0 → Ahead but over budget. Monitor costs. - CPI > 1.0 AND SPI < 1.0 → On budget but behind. Recover schedule. - CPI < 1.0 AND SPI < 1.0 → Behind and over budget. Take corrective action immediately. ## TCPI — To-Complete Performance Index TCPI = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) TCPI is the cost efficiency required for the remaining work to complete on budget. The Contractor will also establish the levels of these areas. The survey shall be undertaken in conjunction with the Engineer. The originals of the survey report and the photographs and negatives shall be handed over to the Engineer within two (2) weeks of the completion of the survey, one (1) copy retained by the Contractor, and one (1) copy handed over to the Employer at the same time. 7.4 Existing Services The Contractor shall undertake all the necessary requirements to identify any existing services that are/potential to be impacted by the associated works in the Contract. Where works are to be undertaken in areas containing existing services, the Contractor shall establish their precise location by hand-digging trenches or by other suitable means such as electronic scanning before laying any adjacent new service. The Contractor shall provide such information regarding existing services to the Engineer and shall include such details on his record and as-built drawings. The Contractor shall liaise with all service providers to confirm and identify all existing services information. In the event of unknown services being discovered during the carrying out of the Works, the Contractor shall immediately inform the Engineer in writing. Payment for diverting or sealing off and abandoning any of these services if necessary or working around the same will only be made where the proviso to (Information and Inspection) the Conditions of Contract applies and even then, only against certified records and subject to the prior authorization of the Engineer with the consent of the Employer. The Contractor shall locate dimensionally on its as-built drawings all services encountered on the Site. 7.5 Third Party Approvals and Notices The Contractor’s responsibility shall be to carry out and complete the whole of the Works to comply as a minimum with the requirements of each and every relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities. Should the Contractor for any reason whatsoever cause such approvals, permits, consents, etc to be withdrawn, the Contractor shall be fully responsible for their reinstatement or re-issuance, irrespective of whether such were originally procured by the Employer. The Contractor shall not commence any element of the project including but not limited to; demolition, excavation, filling, construction or any other works until he has obtained written approval from the relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities, and a copy of that approval has been submitted to the Engineer. The Contractor’s general obligations shall include, without limitation: a. obtaining the necessary approvals/ permits/ consents, etc for excavation works; b. the submission of the Contactor’s temporary works designs and shop drawings to the relevant authorities and Engineer, obtaining both approvals as applicable; c. complying with the relevant requirements of the Employer’s environmental commitments and any future requirements included within the updated environmental approvals with respect to the construction of the works; 189 of 216

# Design Objectives — The 8+1 Whole-Building Goals (WBDG) Reference guidance on the design objectives a high-performance building must balance. Source: WBDG Design Objectives. Best-practice guidance (how to think about a design), not a regulation or binding standard — the project brief and the client's requirements govern priorities. International practice, applies to KSA. These objectives are interdependent: a good design integrates them rather than optimising one in isolation. Grounds how the platform reasons about design trade-offs and brief/BOD analysis. ## The design objectives## The design objectives | Objective | What it means | |---|---| | Accessible | Usable by people of all abilities; accessible routes, entrances, and facilities (universal design). | | Aesthetics | The form, materials, and image of the building and its fit with context. | | Cost-Effective | Best value over the whole life cycle — life-cycle cost, not lowest first cost; value engineering. | | Functional / Operational | Meets the functional programme; systems integration, flexibility, durability, operability. | | Historic Preservation | Respects historic/existing fabric; adaptive reuse where relevant. | | Productive | Occupant comfort, health, and productivity — thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, indoor air quality, ergonomics. | | Resilient | Resists and recovers from hazards and disruptions — robustness, redundancy, adaptability. | | Secure / Safe | Physical security, life safety, fire protection, and natural-hazard mitigation. | | Sustainable | Environmental performance — energy, water, materials, site, and indoor environmental quality (the home of LEED-type goals). |Source: WBDG Design Objectives. ## How they work together - The objectives are **interdependent** — decisions for one affect others (e.g. a sustainability move can improve productivity but change cost). A high-performance design evaluates and balances them, it does not maximise one alone. - **Cost-Effective** is judged on **whole-life cost** (life-cycle cost analysis), not first cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count.cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count. - **Sustainable** is where rating systems (e.g. LEED) live; WBDG frames the goal, the specific rating credits are a separate standard. ## How to use - Use this to explain what each objective covers and that they must be balanced. - The project brief / Owner's Project Requirements set the priority weighting for a specific project — this is the general framework. - When analysing a brief or basis of design, check which objectives are addressed and flag gaps (e.g. resilience or accessibility not mentioned) rather than inventing requirements.

Request for Proposals Large-Scale AI Data Center Campus Development Partnership — Canada April 16, 2026 Introduction Anthropic invites qualified parties to submit proposals for the development of a large-scale AI data center campus in Canada. We are seeking partners with the geographic, political, financial, and subject-matter expertise to deliver a collective 1 GW of critical IT capacity (approximately 1.4 GW total utility load) within Canada by EOY 2028, with initial capacity operational by EOY 2027 and a preference for projects that scale further or deliver faster. This is an initial target that may increase, and we will consider a portfolio of smaller sites across several selected respondents where that optimizes for speed. The objective is to establish a secure campus in Canada that supports advanced AI workloads, contributes to Canadian economic development, adds net-new generation capacity and grid infrastructure, and advances Anthropic's mission. Consistent with Anthropic's published energy affordability commitments in the US, we intend to match our load with net-new generation, fund required grid upgrades, and avoid upward pressure on local electricity prices. A performance specification covering data center technical requirements is being made available to developers as Exhibit A. Respondents should review and address compatibility with those requirements in their proposals. Please note that our requirements diverge notably from a typical hyperscaler cloud data center: our SLA model is a two-tier mixed availability model enabling creative energy solutions; we demand higher rack densities and direct-liquid closed-loop cooling (with a baseline design requiring no make-up water for mechanical heat rejection); and we place a higher premium on speed-to-scale over efficiency/reliability. Respondents proposing a standard hyperscale reference product without addressing these deltas will be disadvantaged. Anthropic is briefing relevant federal and provincial government bodies on this RFP in advance of issuance, and is engaging directly with transmission system operators and regulated utilities in candidate provinces. Selection Framework Anthropic is selecting a long-term partner. We expect this RFP process may culminate in an award before all details of design and timing are fully defined. What is most important is that our development partners have the flexibility and comfort to operate in ambiguous and rapidly evolving requirements environments. We are prioritizing partners who demonstrate: - Control of a well-developed land bank and demonstrated ability to identify and transact on additional land parcels as required. - Deep expertise operating in Canada, with demonstrated ability to navigate land development, entitlement, and permitting processes in-province. - Expertise partnering with utilities and power developers (traditional and renewable) to deploy large-scale campus solutions. We are targeting a minimum 1.4 GW (total utility) campus. We understand there is limited Canadian precedent at this scale and will calibrate qualification criteria accordingly. - Demonstrated experience across the full data center delivery lifecycle: design, supply chain, construction, commissioning, and operations. - Financial and development capabilities aligned to a 1+ GW critical IT scale project. - Ability to meet our security requirements across development, design, and operations —internally or through an aligned third-party partnership. ENVIRONMENT REQUIREMENTS FOR CONTRACTORS GENERAL REQUIREMENTS The scope of works as defined by the tender documents shall, in addition to whatever is described in there, include responsibility for the management and control of all Environmental aspects of the project and the site. Such responsibility shall not be limited to the project but shall extend to the works and activities of all appointed Contractors, including nominated subcontractors, suppliers, and other persons working on or visiting the site. The Employer’s development guidelines reflect the sustainable design, construction, and operation requirements to achieve the following sustainability certifications, as required: • LEED for Cities & Communities Gold certification (version 4.1), with aspirational target of Platinum certification • Mostadam for Communities Gold certification (version 2019), with aspirational target of Platinum certification • SITES Rating System for Sustainable Land Design and Development (version 2) • LEED Building Design and Construction (version 4), certification applicable for specific assets • Mostadam for Residential Buildings Design and Construction (version 2019), certification applicable for specific assets • Mostadam for Commercial Buildings Design and Construction (version 2019), certification applicable for specific assets • Parksmart Gold certification for parking structures The Contractor is responsible for implementing all requirements during construction to meet and achieve the project’s sustainability objectives and targets. Refer to the Sustainability Scope of Service for Contractors for additional details. It is the Contractor’s responsibility to ensure compliance with the statutory environmental requirements of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), as well as other applicable competent authorities. The competent authority for issuance of environmental approvals and permits for projects, as well as specific construction activities the National Center for Environmental Compliance (NCEC). Additional legal requirements may be detailed in approvals or permits issued by other applicable competent authorities including, but not limited to, the following: • Ministryof Environment, Water and Agriculture (MEWA) • National Center for Waste Management (MWAN)

Overview Th document describes the Utility Identification Survey scope of works to be conducted in DII (Area shown in schematic below). The infrastructure package is divided in 3 packages: Package I, Package II and Package III. The below scope of works covers Package I currently but will extend to Packages II and III as optional after agreement with the Client. The information for existing networks for dry and wet utilities has been obtained from the stakeholders/ service providers; however, the accuracy of the information needs to be validated to avoid unforeseen circumstances/ scenarios. This is also fundamental as utility service provisions to existing users will need to be maintained till specific and discrete dates. The existing service connections will be terminated in phases, as the areas become available. The survey should give DGCL a comprehensive picture on the existing utility infrastructure in the highlighted area(s) above which will allow them to identify and quantify to the highest degree of accuracy the amount of utility protection, demolition, diversion needed to carry out the proposed Master Plan in the said zone. Existing Information The available information for the existing utilities with the Client is included herewith and covers the below. It is to be noted that all the information provided as part of the scope of works is to be treated as ‘For Information Only’. Any text/notes on the drawing not relevant will be ignored. HV Network (Appendix ‘A’) MV Network (Appendix ‘B’) LV Network (Appendix ‘C’) Telecom Network including GCC Cable (Appendix ‘D’) Potable Water Network (Appendix ‘E’) Wastewater Network (Appendix ‘F’) In addition to the above, topographical survey of the area is also available, as ‘For Information Only’, which can be made available to the Contractor upon request. Scope To provide a Complete Utility Identification Survey Report for DII Project Site, based on the following list of minimum works but not limited to: Supervision of the works. The Contractor must ensure to liaise with the Construction Supervision supervising its works to ensure that all procedures are stablished in advance of starting the works. Site Visits. Coordinate and conduct a comprehensive site visit for understanding the client’s requests and needs. The Contractor will ensure full compliance with Safety standards as per Contract. As-Built records/drawings. Before starting works on site, the contractor will endeavour all efforts to secure as much information (as-built records and drawings/ any other relevant information) as possible about all relevant buried and above ground assets to be surveyed, by establishing contact with Authorities and Service Providers and report on its findings accordingly. Pre-condition photographic survey. Before starting any works that includes physically impacting existing assets or the ground (excavation, opening of existing structures, excavation of trial trenches, etc), The contractor will ensure to collect extensive photographical evidence of all the surrounding pre-existing conditions of the assets. Trial trenches. Executing various numbers of trial trenches in critically identified locations with focus on recording and identifying all existing buried utilities and/or other various infrastructures, according to the following: Quantity tobe defined by the Contractor and agreed with the CS/Engineer. ADJUST SHOP DRAWINGS PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION TO CONFORM NECESSARY CHANGES. WHERE GROUPS OF SLEEVES ARE LOCATED THEY MUST NOT BE SUCH AS TO AFFECT THE INTEGRITY OF STRUCTURAL MEMBERS. TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS AND WRITTEN INSTRUCTIONS OR DECISIONS OF THE CONSULTANT SHALL TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER THESE NOTES. ALL MATERIALS USED SHALL COMPLY WITH THE REQUIREMENTS OF THE SPECIFIED CODES, STANDARDS AND ORDINANCE OF RELEVANT BUILDING AUTHORITIES UNLESS NOTED OTHERWISE IN THE PROJECT SPECIFICATION AND / OR DRAWINGS. ALL EXISTING SERVICES AND ROAD STRUCTURES WILL HAVE TO BE PROTECTED AT ALL TIMES. CONCRETE SHALL BE CURED BY APPROVED MEANS IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SPECIFICATIONS. OPENING EQUAL OR SMALLER THAN 200 MM WIDTH ARE NOT SHOWN ON THE STRUCTURAL DRAWINGS. SECTION 03 30 00 — CAST-IN-PLACE CONCRETE PART 1 — GENERAL 1.1 SUMMARY A. Section includes cast-in-place concrete for foundations, ground slabs, walls, and pavements, including formwork, reinforcement, mix design, placement, curing, and testing. 1.2 SUBMITTALS A. Mix designs for each concrete class at least 21 days before first pour. B. Reinforcement shop drawings and bar bending schedules. C. Curing method statements per exposed element type. 1.3 QUALITY ASSURANCE A. Batch plant certified to SASO/ASTM C94. One set of three cylinders per 50 m3 or per pour, whichever is more frequent. PART 2 — PRODUCTS 2.1 CONCRETE MATERIALS A. Cement: Type I/II Portland cement, ASTM C150. B. Class C32/40: minimum cementitious content 380 kg/m3, w/c ratio not exceeding 0.45, target slump 100 mm ± 25 mm. C. Blinding class C12/15 may use 20% fly ash replacement. 2.2 REINFORCEMENT A. High-yield deformed bars grade B500B to BS 4449. Cover: 50 mm to ground-contact faces, 40 mm elsewhere unless noted. PART 3 — EXECUTION 3.1 PLACEMENT A. Do not place concrete when ambient temperature exceeds 40 degC unless hot-weather measures are in effect (chilled water, ice, night pours). B. Maximum free-fall height 1.5 m; use tremie or chutes beyond. 3.2 CURING A. Water-cure ground slabs minimum 7 days; membrane curing compound permitted on vertical faces. 3.3 TOLERANCES A. Slab surface flatness FF25 minimum; column verticality within h/500. END OF SECTION
